passage_legs.excerpt: It may be concluded that the pointed hat was worn by both the kings and the gods since Khattushili III is depicted with the pointed hat at Abu Simbel. However the lack of the horn with the hat is important. Because the most important divinity sign is the horned hat in both Anatolia and Mesopotamia. Therefore these figures should be the figures of the kings and princes deified after death, but not of those in life.
passage_legs.normalizations: note markers 21/22 dropped; two-column reading order
passage_legs.supports: entry line 123: horns as the divinity marker; pointed hat alone is not divine status
passage_legs.does_not_support: an exceptionless god-only rule (Ensert records Akurgal/Neve on in-life deification on the facing page)

passage_legs.excerpt: Presently there are two images of Tudkhaliya IV that are confirmed by inscriptions: Tudkhaliya IV is depicted in the king iconography with the cap, the long mantel and the lituus in reliefs 64 and 81 at Yazılıkaya.
passage_legs.supports: entry line 137: royal ceremonial register = cap + long mantle + lituus, distinct from the horned divine headgear
passage_legs.does_not_support: identification of the missing Yazılıkaya statue (Ensert lists competing views, pp. 95–96)

passage_legs.locator: Ensert 2006, printed p. 96, citing van den Hout 1995a: 559 (n. 41)
passage_legs.excerpt: Van den Hout agrees that the Hittite kings were depicted with horny hats only when they were deified after death.
passage_legs.supports: the deity/king identification rule through the still-unread van den Hout 1995 (secondary citation)
passage_legs.does_not_support: that this receipt read van den Hout 1995 itself

passage_legs.excerpt: The mortal, deified while in life, was not allowed to have himself depicted with the horned hat and in god dress
passage_legs.supports: the prohibition reading the entry's brake implies

passage_legs.locator: Ensert 2006, printed p. 96 (Boğazköy House-(chapel)-a stele; her nn. 42–44)
passage_legs.excerpt: The king wears a pointed hat with five pairs of horn, a short skirt and a pair of shoes with the upturned toes and holds a lance resting on the right shoulder (Fig. 3).
passage_legs.supports: a numbered, labelled dated headgear witness: 'Great King Tudkhaliya' with a five-pair horned pointed hat
passage_legs.does_not_support: which Tudhaliya (her text leaves Tudhaliya I or later open)

passage_legs.locator: Ensert 2006, printed p. 96, n. 40 (citing van den Hout 1995a: 561)
passage_legs.excerpt: Van den Hout explains the depictions of Tudkhaliya IV as follows: In relief 64 with the Sun God dressing he is the supreme judge and in the seal impression from Ugarit with the Storm God dressing he is the supreme warrior.
passage_legs.supports: the deity/king register-switching reading behind entry line 137's 'role-specific dress'
passage_legs.does_not_support: that the Ugarit seal's small god figure is Tudhaliya IV (Ensert argues Murshili II)

passage_legs.excerpt: the kings are depicted with unmistakably divine attributes, specifically with conical hats adorned with horns that have been used as symbols of divinity in the Near East since the third millennium bc
passage_legs.supports: a dated horizon for the horn motif (third millennium BCE Near East) without equating it with Hattic evidence
passage_legs.does_not_support: any claim that third-millennium Anatolian headgear looked the same

passage_legs.excerpt: The Südburg monument in Hattuša depicts a Šuppiluliuma in the martial outfit wearing a horned hat. Originally dated to the reign of Šuppiluliuma II, there is now an intense academic debate surrounding the patronage of this monument.
passage_legs.supports: a documented royal figure in the horned hat — i.e. the rule's exception space, as the entry's brake requires
passage_legs.does_not_support: a secure attribution of the Südburg figure

passage_legs.excerpt: As seals would be in circulation during the lifetime of the king, this particular seal of Muršili III calls into question his earthly nature, and may mean that Muršili III started a tradition of incorporating aspects of divine iconography into royal representation while he still reigned as a living king. … The divine status of Tudhaliya IV as symbolized with the horned caps is visible even in the Umarmungsszene, such as on his cylinder seal, where both the god and the king are wearing matching hats and outfits.
passage_legs.normalizations: two sentences joined; note marker 90 dropped
passage_legs.supports: the strongest image behind entry line 123 (god and king in matching horned caps); documents in-life exceptions
passage_legs.does_not_support: that every royal horned-cap image implies lifetime deification

passage_legs.excerpt: In the representation of Tudhaliya IV in Yazılıkaya 64, the king is shown standing on two mountains, a symbol of divinity, while his name in hieroglyphic Luwian stretches below a drawing of the winged sun disk (Figure 8). … Emirgazi altars, erected during the reign of Tudhaliya IV, mention votive offerings to be made to him, making it possible to suggest that the king was already deified before his death.
passage_legs.normalizations: two sentences joined; note markers 88/89 dropped
passage_legs.supports: dated, labelled identification of relief 64; a textual basis for in-life deification
passage_legs.does_not_support: that the Emirgazi evidence is unambiguous

passage_legs.locator: Gilibert 2015, printed p. 144, n. 46 (Malatya, Relief E, PUGNUS-mili cycle)
passage_legs.excerpt: one of them is bearded and wears a horned, pointed hat; the other one is beardless, wears no hat, and sports long hair styled in peculiar curls. The PUGNUS-mili with beard and horned hat may be the dead grandfather of PUGNIS-mili (II), who sponsored the relief cycle (Brown 2008: 303).
passage_legs.normalizations: repository spelling 'PUGNIS-mili' in the second occurrence (sic)
passage_legs.supports: the later Neo-Hittite comparator: horned pointed hat = dead/divine ancestor, hatless = living ruler — the same distinction, post-1200 BCE
passage_legs.does_not_support: that this Iron Age relief may be used as Empire-period evidence

passage_legs.excerpt: all of them dating before the destruction of the 'Porta Schaeffer' at the end of the 11th/beginning of the 10th century BC.
passage_legs.supports: a date for the dated Neo-Hittite headgear witness the round-8 limit asked for
passage_legs.does_not_support: a single fixed date for every Malatya relief (the note proposes a re-sequencing)

passage_legs.excerpt: This paper focuses on monumental art decorating public gates at Karkemiš as a key to understanding the negotiation of political power in the period between 1200 and 950 BC.
passage_legs.supports: the Iron Age frame that keeps this comparator from being back-projected (entry line 49)

passage_legs.excerpt: The association with Alacahöyük (Arinna?) is irresistible. In the third millennium BC already, before the growth of the importance of nearby Ḫattusa, Alacahöyük had been the seat of a local dynasty. It peaked in prosperity in the EB III period, which is how the royal tombs there are dated.
passage_legs.supports: a dated pre-Hittite dynastic seat at the same site as the EB III 'royal' tombs
passage_legs.does_not_support: an ethnic 'Hattic' label for that dynasty

passage_legs.excerpt: the openwork headbands from Alacahüyük that probably functioned as a crown (Koşay 1938: Pl. 82; 1951: Pl. 129; Muscarella 2003: 280). … the diadems from Alacahöyük were found in a restricted number of elite burials and were clearly attributes of power and elevated social position. … Two of the five diadems from Alacahöyük had additional strips hanging from the headband (Hickman 2008: 249), representing a specifically local tradition.
passage_legs.normalizations: three excerpts joined (main text + n. 7); artifact spells 'Alacahüyük' at the first locus, 'Alacahöyük' elsewhere
passage_legs.supports: the earlier comparator as dated objects: EB III gold diadems/headbands, elite-only, power attributes
passage_legs.does_not_support: horns, a cap form, or a Hattic attribution

passage_legs.excerpt: was carried on in the later 3rd millennium BC (a more exact dating was impossible in most cases)
passage_legs.supports: the date range for this object class (with the author's own caveat)

passage_legs.excerpt: we know diadems since the 3rd Millennium onwards from several archaeological sites, most of the time out of funeral context. … Diadems can be decorated with techniques of repoussé, engravings or open worked decorations. They are known from Arslantepe … as well as from Alacahöyük … Fig. 1: Alacahöyük Tomb A, Diadem: Photo DBM, Yalçın.
passage_legs.supports: an object-level, illustrated (photographic plate) pre-Hittite headgear witness from a museum publication

passage_legs.excerpt: The Hittite received from the Hattians not only the gods for their official pantheon together with the related cultual ceremonials, but also the belief that the land had to supply its gods with food consigned yearly by those who represented the central administration in each of the major centres.
passage_legs.supports: what the scholarly Hattic-inheritance discussion actually covers here: cult and administration
passage_legs.does_not_support: any Hattian headgear term or image — the 'earlier Hattic comparator' leg stays partial
